display: flex creates a flex container. flex-direction: row makes the main axis horizontal here, so align-items: center centers vertically. align-self: flex-end moves only .two to the cross-axis end. These meanings follow axes, not permanently horizontal or vertical directions.
Use container alignment for a row of unequal controls, then override a special item only when useful. This example fixes horizontal writing and LTR; writing mode and flex direction affect the axes.
Center the first item on the row’s cross axis and align the second to its end.
after: Flexbox has a main axis, the direction items are arranged, and a cross axis at a right angle to it. `align-items` lines items up on the cross axis. `align-self` changes that alignment for one item.
`align-items: center` centers the items vertically here. The `.two` rule overrides that choice for the second item. `align-self: flex-end` puts only that item at the bottom edge.

If the direction changes to `column`, the main axis becomes vertical here. The cross axis becomes horizontal. The same alignment settings would center the first item left to right and place the second at the right edge.
Alignment follows the axes, so `align-items` does not always mean vertical alignment. First check the flex direction and the writing direction. Then decide where the cross axis starts and ends.
Keep a row for the project. Center the first item vertically and put the second at the bottom. Run the checks and look at both positions.
